food.text: Among Indigenous peoples of North America, maize was the most important food, with beans and squash also highly regarded. Known as the "Three Sister Crops", the three were typically planted together, supporting each other as they grew.

The most important Indigenous American crops included maize, beans, squash, pumpkins, sunflowers, wild rice, sweet potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, peanuts, avocados, potatoes and chocolate. The word maize itself comes from the Taíno name for the plant.
In the Southwest, the Puebloan people turned to agriculture, holding small farms along the Rio Grande in New Mexico. Their diet consisted of corn, beans, and squash.

Butternuts found at L'Anse aux Meadows show that Norse voyages reached south into the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, as far as the St. Lawrence River and parts of New Brunswick — the northern limit for both butternut and wild grapes.

Butternuts and wood fragments were found in the Norse remains at L'Anse aux Meadows, a site dating to around 1021. They came from plants not native to Newfoundland, which suggests the Norse made expeditions to the continental mainland.
Not every Southwestern group took up farming. The Navajo, Apache, and Utes retained their hunter-gatherer roots, living alongside Puebloan farmers who relied on corn, beans, and squash.

Southeastern Native Americans made corn into hominy by liming it with an alkaline salt, a technique known as nixtamalization. Corn was also ground into meal, and both forms helped shape the later Southern diet.
Chokecherries were an important crop, mostly for the Blackfoot and Cheyenne tribes, alongside maize, beans, and squash, which were the most valued foods among the peoples of North America.

Southeastern Indians boiled their beans and field peas and cured meat by smoking it over hickory coals. Southern cooks later kept both habits, and many early settlers were taught Southeastern Native American cooking methods.

L'Anse aux Meadows, dating to around 1021, had no stables, farms or cemeteries, so it probably served as an overwintering base rather than a permanent community. Butternuts and wood found there came from plants not native to Newfoundland.

art.text: Southeastern Ceremonial Complex motifs have been found on marine shell, ceramics, chert, carved stone, and copper, including the Etowah plates and the Wulfing cache. Many other materials were probably used too, but have not survived the centuries.

Pueblo Bonito, the largest Chacoan great house, covers almost 2 acres and has at least 650 rooms, with parts of it four stories high. Its massive masonry walls are up to 3 ft thick. Once complete, its scale rivaled that of the Colosseum.

Woodhenge III at Cahokia had 48 posts and was 410 feet in diameter, built in approximately 1000 CE. From its central pole, the sun would have appeared to rise from Fox Mound and its summit temple at the winter solstice.

A pair of shell gorgets so similar they seem made by the same artist were found in southeast Missouri and at Spiro Mounds in Oklahoma, hundreds of miles apart. This suggests such items were gifts or exchange goods across a wide region.

Moundville's 29 platform mounds surround a rectangular plaza. Archaeologists interpret this plan as a sociogram, an architectural depiction of a social order in which the size and arrangement of paired earthen mounds represented the ranked positions of clans.

Ancestral Puebloans in the northern part of their lands, from about 500 to 1300 CE, commonly decorated pottery with black-painted designs on white or light gray backgrounds. The decoration is characterized by fine hatching, using mineral-based paint on a chalky background.

Pueblo Bonito is divided into two sections by a wall precisely aligned to run north–south, bisecting the central plaza. A great kiva was placed on either side of the wall, creating a symmetrical pattern common to many Chacoan great houses.

The Mitchell Log, the largest marker post recovered from Cahokia, is 11 feet tall and weighs 2,200 pounds today. Radiocarbon and isotope analysis found the tree was felled around 1124 and carried about 100 miles to the site, possibly through Mississippi backwater channels.

Surviving paintings with Southeastern Ceremonial Complex imagery include one on a baked clay floor at Wickliffe Mounds and others in caves, notably Mud Glyph Cave in Tennessee. Images include winged warriors, horned snakes, stylized birds, maces, and arrows. Their underground location probably reflects Mississippian myth about the possibly sacred precincts beneath the earth.

Cahokia's woodhenges are reflected in a stylized cross in circle motif on ceremonial beakers. One prominent beaker, found in an offertory pit near the winter solstice post pit, has markers for the winter sunrise and sunset positions, plus radiating lines that probably symbolized the rays of the sun.

literature.text: The Vinland sagas are two Icelandic texts, the Saga of the Greenlanders and the Saga of Erik the Red, written independently of each other in the early 13th century. They were written down between 1220 and 1280 and describe events from around 970 to 1030. They hold the most complete information available on Norse exploration of the Americas.

The Great Law of Peace is the oral constitution of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, established circa 1102 CE among the Five Nations. It was conceived by Dekanawidah, known as the Great Peacemaker, and his spokesman Hiawatha. Symbols on wampum belts served as mnemonic devices for storytellers who kept the law alive.

The Saga of the Greenlanders recounts events that purportedly happened around 1000, yet it survives only in the late 14th century Flateyjarbók manuscript. It relates six expeditions to North America, led by figures such as Bjarni Herjolfsson, Leif Erikson and Freydís Eiríksdóttir. Along the way Thorvald is killed by the natives in combat and Thorstein dies of an illness, and Freydís slaughters the crew of the brothers Helgi and Finnbogi, killing the five women left alive with an axe herself. Together with the Saga of Erik the Red, it is a main source on Norse colonization.

The name Vinland means 'Wineland' and is attributed to the grapevines found when Leif Erikson arrived in North America. However, some scholars believe the word instead refers to pasture or meadow. The sagas also contradict each other on details, such as who first sighted land and how many voyages were taken.

Despite its title, the Saga of Erik the Red mainly chronicles the expedition of Thorfinn Karlsefni and his wife Gudrid. It is closer to medieval travel narratives than to other Sagas of Icelanders. It is also unusual in focusing on a woman, Gudrid.

According to Haudenosaunee oral tradition, Tadodaho was an Onondaga leader widely feared as a sorcerer. He was said to have a twisted body and matted hair, to kill his enemies from a distance without seeing them, and to rule by fear, raiding the Cayuga and attacking the Seneca. Three times he broke Hiawatha's attempts to call a peace council, and each time one of Hiawatha's daughters died, deaths blamed on Tadodaho's powers. The Great Peacemaker and Hiawatha finally persuaded him to accept the Great Law of Peace, and after being healed of his evil ways he became a founding member of the Grand Council, serving as firekeeper and chair.

The Saga of Erik the Red survives in two manuscripts, Hauksbók from the 14th century and Skálholtsbók from the 15th. Haukr Erlendsson and his assistants are thought to have revised the Hauksbók text, making it less colloquial and more stylish. The Skálholtsbók version appears to be a faithful but somewhat careless copy of the original.

In the Saga of Erik the Red, the Norse in Markland meet five Skrælings. The three adults sink into the ground and escape, but the Norse capture the two boys and baptize them. The boys reportedly say that the Skrælings are cave-dwellers ruled by two kings named Avaldamon and Avaldidida, and mention a nearby country that the saga writer thought was the legendary Hvítramannaland.

The Saga of Erik the Red contains an unusual amount of pagan practice, sorcery and ghost stories. It has been used as a source on Old Norse religion, especially the prophecy scene with Thorbjorg. It is often described as unreliable, and one scholar called it a polemical attack on pagan practices supposedly still prevalent around the year 1000 in Greenland.

The Great Law of Peace is divided into 117 articles and presented as part of a narrative noting laws and ceremonies to be performed at prescribed times. The nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy are symbolized by an eastern white pine tree, called the Tree of Peace. The laws were first recorded by means of wampum, shell-bead belts encoding the message in pictograms.

In 1956, Jón Jóhannesson dated the Saga of the Greenlanders to around 1200, making it older than the Saga of Erik the Red. He noticed that Erik the Red's saga calls a descendant of Karlsefni and Gudrid 'Bishop Brandr the First', while the Greenlanders saga says only 'Bishop Brandr'. That suggested the second author never needed to tell two bishops apart.

science.text: At a site called Nanook, a stone crucible had once used very high heat to melt metal alloys like bronze. Radiocarbon dating placed it broadly between 754 BC and 1367 AD. Its finder, Sutherland, said it may be the earliest evidence of high-temperature nonferrous metalworking in North America north of Mexico.

At Cahokia, builders raised a series of large timber circles, thought to date between 900 and 1100 CE, each larger and with more posts than the one before. Archaeologists nicknamed them 'woodhenges' and have used them to study how Cahokia's people may have tracked the sun.

Chacoan builders quarried sandstone blocks and hauled timber from great distances, assembling 15 major complexes. These stayed the largest buildings ever built in North America until the 19th century.

The Ancestral Puebloans had a distinct knowledge of celestial sciences, and it found form in their architecture. The kiva, a congregational space used mostly for ceremonies, was an integral part of the community structure.

At Nanook, Sutherland's team found whetstones used to sharpen blades. Metal fragments in them included bronze, brass and smelted iron, in the medieval European metallurgy style. There is no evidence that Indigenous North Americans smelted alloys, while the Norse regularly did.

Woodhenge III at Cahokia had 48 posts and was 410 feet across, and it was built around 1000 CE. Its posts stand 7 degrees 30 minutes apart, and its central post sits 5.6 feet off true center. This offset lined up perimeter posts with the winter and summer solstice sunrises, correcting for Cahokia's latitude.

Pueblo Bonito covered almost 2 acres and had at least 650 rooms, with parts four stories high. Its builders used core-and-veneer construction, which needed massive masonry walls up to 3 feet thick. A wall precisely aligned north to south bisected its central plaza.
Around AD 1000, Mesa Verde builders moved from pole-and-adobe construction to stone masonry. The thick-walled stone buildings could be built higher and offered more residential and storage capacity.

The Woodhenge site was found during salvage archaeology by Warren Wittry in the early 1960s, ahead of a highway interchange. He noticed arcs of equally spaced post holes and guessed they were whole circles, possibly a calendar for tracking solstices and equinoxes. One circle was rebuilt in 1985.

Repeated floods in the mid-14th century deepened the Salt River bed and destroyed the heads of Hohokam canals, so they had to be extended farther upstream. More flooding then removed those extensions, leaving hundreds of miles of canals virtually useless.

The largest Chacoan roads were built at the same time as many great houses, between 1000 and 1125 CE. They included the Great North Road, the South Road and the Coyote Canyon Road. Some stretches lead to natural features such as springs, lakes and mountain tops.

At a site called Nanook, archaeologists found whetstones holding fragments of bronze, brass and smelted iron in a medieval European metallurgy style. A stone crucible there had once melted metal alloys at very high heat. The Norse regularly smelted alloys, but there is no evidence that Indigenous North Americans did.

Researchers dated the Mitchell Log, the largest marker post recovered at Cahokia, using radiocarbon dating and strontium isotope analysis. The tree was felled around 1124 CE at about 194 years old, and was carried roughly 100 miles to the site. It may have traveled along Mississippi backwater channels rather than over land.

Dendrochronology shows the last tree felled for construction on Mesa Verde was cut in 1281. The 13th century brought 69 years of below-average rainfall, and after 1260 "tens of thousands of people" emigrated or died from starvation. A severely dry period from 1276 to 1299, which archaeologists call the "Great Drought", ended seven hundred years of continuous human occupation. Competition between clans turned into intense warfare, and violence peaked between 1275 and 1285, with partly burned villages, one village that appears to have been massacred, and victims who were scalped, dismembered and cannibalized.

politics.text: Recent archaeological evidence shows that the elite family buried at the great house of Pueblo Bonito practiced matrilineal succession. Room 33, the richest burial ever excavated in the Southwest, served as a crypt for one powerful lineage traced through the female line for approximately 330 years.

The Haudenosaunee Confederacy joined five Iroquoian peoples south of the Great Lakes into "The Great League of Peace". It was established before European contact. Many archaeologists and anthropologists believe it formed about 1450, though some argue for dates as early as 1142.

Cahokia was the largest and most influential urban settlement of the Mississippian culture. At its apex around 1100 AD, it covered about 6 square miles, included about 120 earthworks, and had a population of between 15,000 and 20,000 people.

The Haudenosaunee Council valued unanimity in public acts. Under the account recorded in 1855, no treaty was binding unless ratified by 75% of the male voters and 75% of the mothers of the nation. This double supermajority made the Confederacy a de facto consensus government.

The Great Peacemaker established a council of clan and village chiefs to govern the confederacy. Men held the chief positions through their mother's line, but clan mothers ruled on the fitness of chiefs and could depose any that they opposed. Most council decisions were made by consensus, with each representative having an equal voice.

Around 1160 to 1170, a large walled residential compound in Cahokia's East St. Louis precinct was burned down, along with multiple ritual structures filled with an unusual density of stone tools, exotic materials and pots of shelled maize. This possibly represented unrest in response to 12th century inequalities. Around 1175 people built the first large central palisade around Cahokia's core. That palisade was later rebuilt several times around ever smaller parts of the city as the population shrank, and bastioned palisades almost always indicate warfare.

During Cahokia's Moorehead phase, from 1200 to 1300, mound construction continued at a lesser rate and many earlier mounds were ritually capped. Scholars have taken this as a time when centralized political structures were weakening and religious practices were re-evaluated. Some theories propose conquest by outside peoples as the main reason for the collapse, pointing to a defensive wooden stockade with watchtowers and several 13th century burned villages in the Illinois River Valley to the north. By 1350 the city was abandoned, and the population had already fallen by half or more by the middle of the 13th century.

The founding date of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy is debated because of an oral account in which a violent conflict among the Seneca stopped when the sun darkened and the day seemed to turn to night. Scholars have widely supported 1451 AD, a known solar eclipse, as the likely founding date, while some favor 1142, when another eclipse was documented. In 1982 archeologist Dean Snow said that evidence from mainstream archeology did not support a founding before 1350 AD.

Droughts struck Illinois twice between 1150 and 1200, and a third came around 1275, bringing much political instability. Many Central Mississippians left, and immigration to the Nashville area peaked around 1275. Most of these Cahokian groups were likely families returning to ancestral lands rather than invading migrants.

philosophy.text: The Great Law of Peace is the oral constitution of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, conceived by Dekanawidah, known as the Great Peacemaker, and his spokesman Hiawatha. Its laws are divided into 117 articles. The nations of the confederacy are symbolized by an eastern white pine tree, called the Tree of Peace.

The Mississippian peoples of the Eastern Woodlands were characterized by theocratic governance, population centers, and the predominance of maize agriculture. This set them apart from the preceding Woodland peoples, whose mound-building was more limited to burial mounds. Their flat-topped platform mounds still carried a summit structure that appears to be uniquely Mississippian.

Archaeologists think the Cahokia Woodhenge was a solar calendar that marked equinox and solstice sunrises for the agricultural cycle and religious observances. At the equinoxes, the sun appears to rise from the front of Monks Mound when seen from the center of the timber circle.

According to tradition, Hiawatha was once a wild man and a cannibal, known as "the man who eats humans." When Dekanawidah came to his cabin, he climbed onto the roof and looked down through the smoke hole at a large kettle of water set for cooking a meal of human flesh. When Hiawatha came home, he looked into the water and saw Dekanawidah's face reflected back, which he thought was his own. He felt astonishment and then shame, for it was not the face of one who killed and ate his fellow men, and he accepted the Great Law of Peace.

The Great Law of Peace was first recorded and passed on by wampum, shell-bead belts that encoded the message in a sequence of pictograms. The symbols on the belts functioned as mnemonic devices for storytellers. The law was not translated into English until the 19th century.

Archaeological interpretations of the Chaco road system are divided between an economic purpose and a symbolic, ideological or religious role. Chaco Culture National Historical Park is one of the UNESCO sites credited to the Pueblos.

During Cahokia's Moorehead phase, from 1200 to 1300, people stopped building and using the older T and L shaped ritual buildings and large circular rotundas. Many earlier mounds were ritually capped and never modified again. This has been taken as a time when centralized political structures were weakening and religious practices thought essential were re-evaluated.

The great roads of Chaco Canyon were built at the same time as many of the great houses, from 1000 to 1125 CE. Some lead to natural features such as springs, lakes, mountain tops, and pinnacles. Archaeologists are divided between an economic purpose and a symbolic, ideological or religious role for the road system.

At the Spiro site, artists of the Caddoan Mississippian culture made works expressing their complex spiritual beliefs. Many artifacts there featured the symbolism of the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex, a multiregional trade and religious network.

The largest marker post recovered from Cahokia is the Mitchell Log. In 2025, University of Arizona researchers found the tree had been felled around 1124 CE and moved about 100 miles to the site. Its timber circle is thought to have been a solar calendar.

As a mark of respect, some Haudenosaunee avoid using the Great Peacemaker's personal name, Deganawida, except in special circumstances. By tradition he founded the Haudenosaunee Confederacy along with Jigonhsasee and Hiawatha.

culture.text: Between 900 and 1150, Chaco Canyon was a major cultural center for the Ancestral Puebloans. Chacoans quarried sandstone blocks and hauled timber from great distances to assemble 15 major complexes. These remained the largest buildings ever built in North America until the 19th century.

Norse settlements on Greenland's western coast peaked at a population of 2,000 to 3,000. The colonists lived by pastoral farming on scattered coastal fjords and exported mainly walrus ivory to Europe.

Around 1000 CE, the Thule people replaced the Dorset culture in the Canadian Arctic. The Dorset walrus ivory carvings were primarily ceremonial, while the art of the Thule was more decorative in character.
culture.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

culture.text: Indigenous North American societies emphasized egalitarianism. European cultures only began arriving after 1492, from the south through Spanish exploration and conquest and from the east.

L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, dating to around 1021, could house between 30 and 160 people. It had no stables, farms or cemeteries, so it probably served as an overwintering base and ship-repair station rather than a permanent community.

In 1126 the Norse settlers of Greenland requested a bishop, headquartered at a bishopric established in Garðar. In 1261 they accepted the overlordship of the Norwegian king, yet kept their own law and were almost completely politically independent after 1349, the time of the Black Death.
The Yup'ik of Alaska have a long tradition of carving masks for use in shamanic rituals. It is one of many Indigenous art forms tied to ceremony and belief.
culture.source_title: Visual arts of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

culture.text: Many Native American tribes held war captives as slaves before European colonization, and treatment varied widely: captives could be enslaved for life, killed, or adopted. Warrior captives were sometimes made to undergo ritual mutilation or torture that could end in death, as part of a spiritual grief ritual for relatives slain in battle, and captives were also sometimes tortured in religious rites that sometimes involved ritual cannibalism. The Iroquoian peoples often adopted captives, but for religious reasons such adoptions were delayed until the proper spiritual times.
culture.source_title: Slavery among Native Americans in the United States

culture.text: Greenland's Western Settlement was abandoned around 1350, and the last bishop at Garðar died in 1377. The most recent radiocarbon date found in Norse settlements as of 2002 was 1430, give or take 15 years.

Some Native American groups staked themselves in gambling when they had nothing else to wager. Losing put them into servitude for a short time, or in some cases for life. During times of famine, some Native Americans would also temporarily sell their children to obtain food.
culture.source_title: Slavery among Native Americans in the United States

culture.text: The last written mention of the Greenland Norse is a marriage recorded in 1408. After that, no written records mention the settlers, although archaeologists have found one house possibly in use as late as 1409.
